title: Stopped Whilst in Progress
logline: A carved stone platform on three terraces in a river bend, known by a name that a colonial archaeologist glossed as 'the temple to get redemption' and recorded, as the work of a king said to have asked his monks how a father's killing could be undone and to have been told it could not. The killing is attested only in a chronicle written about a hundred and seventy years later and doubted by that chronicle's own translator; the building beside it has finished carving on one side and half-dressed slabs lying where the work stopped.
human_question: When I keep going back over something I did, am I paying for it, or only making it heavier?

place.what_kind_of_place: A ruined sixteenth-century Hindu shrine of a short-lived lowland kingdom, on a tongue of high ground formed by a sharp bend in a fast wet-zone river. It is reached over a wide ditch spanned by five massive stone slabs, each more than four metres long, then up three broad earthwork terraces skirted by the river on one side and at the rear, the highest revetted in six courses of smoothed stone with a deeply undercut coping. On top stands only the platform of the shrine itself: a stepped, recessed plan in Dravidian manner, its mouldings carved with water-leaves, small conventional arch-motifs and a running fillet of circular and star-shaped flowers, a water spout finished as a lotus, two small slabs carved with brimming vases, and a single door jamb still upright. The chamber inside the walls was never more than about five metres square. Whether a temple ever rose above the platform is not known. It is a fenced archaeological site, not a place of worship: no image, no priest, no offerings are recorded there.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Two finishes of stone in one place. On the platform, carving of a delicacy that the surveyor who measured it in the 1890s said must be seen to be appreciated: a garland of flowers two inches deep carried all the way round a wall, a spout that ends in a drooping lotus. Around it, as he recorded them, the pieces the masons never finished: fragments of a massive volute balustrade, a huge oval threshold stone, and many half-dressed slabs lying about. Wet, the carved stone goes from grey to near-black and every incised line fills; the half-dressed stone just goes dark. Below, the river comes round the tongue of land on two sides, brown and loud after rain, and a five-slab bridge crosses the old ditch on the way in.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Rain and the river, and nothing else. A squall arrives in the canopy before it reaches the platform, soaks the stone in minutes and passes; the river rises and browns through the afternoon. The carved and the uncarved surfaces take the water differently, and that difference is the film's whole visual argument. No person is filmed and nothing is staged.
place.when_it_looks_best: An inter-monsoon afternoon, April to May or October to November, when convective squalls come through in the early afternoon and the river is up by late afternoon. The film is shot in the rain and in the half hour after it. Direct sun is the one condition to avoid: it flattens the shallow carving and dries the stone. The driest month, January, is the fallback, with a lower river and no darkening of the stone.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The circling film. The ground camera goes round the platform of a ruined shrine, low, on a 35–50 mm lens, in a series of passes cut together rather than one move: each pass begins at the same lotus-tipped spout, each one later in the squall, the stone a shade darker each time round. Nothing is ever shown whole from a height inside the enclosure. The film opens and closes on water, with a low drone following a river in spate round the bend that holds the ruin. Its payoff is a cut, not a shot: from the finished garland of stone flowers on the platform to a slab in the grass that was squared and never carved, the rain lying in its rough surface. Then out of the circle and down to the river.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same passes become an argument about going over a thing again. A later chronicle puts a question in a king's mouth, how the killing of his father could be undone, and puts an answer in his monks' mouths, that it could not be. The handbook these films follow says something about regret that neither the question nor the answer contains: that recalling a wrong is not the fault, that the scorching over it is, and that the scorching, which many take for something that thins the wrong, makes a small wrong heavy. The circling is the voice going over the story as the literature has for four centuries; the cut to the uncarved slab is where the circling stops. The film never says what the king felt, never says the killing happened, and never lets the stopped building read as a verdict on anyone.

sequence.on_screen: Mid-afternoon, rain coming. A low drone follows a brown, fast river as it swings hard round a tongue of forested high ground; in the trees on top, for a moment, the edge of a stone platform. The drone keeps going with the river and does not climb.
sequence.voice: In a bend of this river there is a platform of carved stone, all that stands of a shrine. The name people use for it was written down in 1904 by a colonial archaeologist, who took it from local tradition and translated it as 'the temple to get redemption'. He also wrote down why it was said to have been built. That reason is a story about a king and his father. No chronicle mentions the building at all.

sequence.on_screen: On the platform, the first pass. Low, 50 mm, moving slowly along the carved basement from the lotus-tipped water spout: water-leaf mouldings, a fillet of circular and star-shaped flowers, stone still pale before the rain.
sequence.voice: The accusation comes from a later chronicle, written about a hundred and seventy years after the events, most probably by a senior monk at another king's court. It says that Rājasiṃha slew his father Māyādunnē. It says that one day he asked the elders how the crime could be undone, and that they told him it was impossible. Another chronicle, the Rājāvaliya, records Māyādunnē's death in one sentence and gives no cause. Wilhelm Geiger, who translated the later chronicle, added a footnote: whether this man really killed his father may be doubted.

sequence.on_screen: The rain arrives. Second pass, starting again at the spout: the same mouldings going dark, water standing in the flower fillet, the single upright door jamb, the two small slabs carved with brimming vases.
sequence.voice: Then the chronicle reaches for a simile. It says he was like a poisonous snake struck with a stick. Nobody who wrote that had seen him. It is the handbooks' own image for hate, the one the commentaries use to define it, and the longer book these films follow uses it too. So the page is doing something worth noticing: a learned writer, generations later, is assembling a mind for a king out of the textbook. This film goes the other way round. It keeps the textbook and leaves the king's mind alone.

sequence.on_screen: Third pass, the squall at its heaviest. The camera goes round the same corner of the platform and past the same spout, now running; the stone almost black; the far side of the platform lost in rain.
sequence.voice: Here is what the longer book actually says about going back over a wrong. Remembering it is not the fault. The fault is the scorching that comes afterwards. Many people, it says, take that scorching, the grieving and repenting over what they did, for a good quality that thins the wrong. It does the opposite: it fouls the mind again and again, and it makes a small wrong heavy. And grieving over good you did not do produces no good. It only weakens the mind that was ready to do some.

sequence.on_screen: Out of the circle. Down the terraces, a static frame on each, and across the old ditch on its bridge of five long slabs, the ditch full and moving into the river on one side.
sequence.voice: The books are precise about where this kind of regret lives. The longer one says it arises only in the two minds rooted in aversion, and each of those always comes with a painful feeling. The shorter one lists the occasions on which that mind arises, and among them is sorrow over a great wrong done by one's own hand. So in these texts regret of this kind is not conscience at work. It is a pushing-away, turned on the past.

sequence.on_screen: Back on the platform as the rain eases. A close frame on the finished fillet of stone flowers, wet and sharp, then a cut to a squared slab lying in the grass below the terrace, rough, never carved, the rain lying in its surface.
sequence.voice: The archaeologist who measured the platform found the masons' work lying where it stopped: pieces of a huge balustrade, a great oval threshold stone, many half-dressed slabs. The work, he wrote, was suddenly stopped whilst in progress, and what the architect meant may never be known. The tradition he recorded gives the building an ending of its own, a punishment. This film does not repeat it. A stopped piece of work is evidence that the work stopped, and of nothing more.

sequence.on_screen: Late afternoon, the rain gone. The low drone again, picking up the river where it leaves the bend and going downstream with it, the tongue of land and its platform behind, the water high and fast.
sequence.voice: The chronicle's monks are made to say that what was done cannot be undone, and the longer book does not disagree. But it adds the part that neither the chronicle nor the building has in it. Remembering is allowed. What it asks is only that the strength not go into the scorching, because that strength is the same strength that does the good still possible today.

concept_merge.why_together: C022 supplies the teaching the film turns on, and C007 supplies where the teaching puts it. Pradeepika defines kukkucca as the scorching that arises afterwards over wrong done and good left undone, and its worked example is a man who did wrong in the pride of youth and hears the teaching in old age [C022-P:L141]; Margaya's definition is the same in one sentence [C022-M:L49]. Then the line the film is built on: recalling a past wrong is not kukkucca; many take the grieving and repentance over it for a good quality that thins the wrong, but it fouls the mind again and again and makes a small wrong heavy, and regret over good not done produces no good but weakens the mind that was ready to do it [C022-P:L143]. C007 then fixes the jurisdiction: envy, stinginess and remorse arise only in the two hate-rooted minds [C007-P:L51], which always come with painful feeling [C007-P:L25–L28]; and Margaya's list of occasions for those minds includes sorrow over great wrongs done by one's own hand [C007-M:L19]. The site supplies the rest in its own documents: a chronicle that stages exactly the question C022 answers (how can this be undone?) and then describes the questioner with Pradeepika's own simile for hate, the snake struck with a stick [C022-P:L119]; and a building whose name was glossed as a redemption-temple and whose surveyor found it stopped mid-work.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the handbook's account of regret is not the chronicle's. The chronicle has a question and a refusal; the handbook has a third thing, a claim about what going over a wrong does, and it cuts against both the king's supposed hope and a modern viewer's instinct that feeling bad is a kind of payment. C022 alone would make this a sermon about guilt with a ruin behind it. C007 alone would make it a film about an angry king, which is exactly the portrait the floor forbids and the chronicle supplies. Together they move the whole film onto the classification: regret of this kind is a hate-rooted state, aversion turned on one's own past, and the source's alternative to it is neither forgetting nor being forgiven but not spending one's strength on the scorching. The site adds what no analogy could: the recorded question and refusal, a textbook simile inside a chronicle, and a payment in stone that was never finished for a debt that is not established.

concept_links.why: Remorse, kukkucca, is the eleventh of the fourteen and the film's subject. Pradeepika's definition and example, the scorching that comes afterwards over wrong done and good left undone in a man who acted in the pride of youth [C022-P:L141], and Margaya's one-line definition [C022-M:L49], set the register. The film is built on the digest's most surprising line: recalling a past wrong is not the fault; the grieving and repentance that many take for a good quality that thins the wrong in fact fouls the mind again and again and makes a small wrong heavy, and regret over good not done only weakens the mind that could do good now [C022-P:L143]. Both does_not_transfer readings are handled on screen: 'remorse purifies' is refused in beat 4 in the source's own terms, and the opposite slogan, 'never feel bad', is refused in beats 4 and 7 by keeping the source's separation of recalling, which is allowed, from scorching. The exemption question was read at the source and decided: plain remembering is exempt (L143 says so in terms), and the film places the viewer's own recollection of the story in that exempt case. The chronicle's simile for the king is Pradeepika's simile for hate, the snake struck with a stick [C022-P:L119]; the film uses that line only to show the chronicle building a mind out of the handbook, never to describe the king. Pradeepika's claim that strong remorse can be lifted only with the help of Buddhas, paccekabuddhas or arahants [C022-P:L151] is flagged in the digest for expert checking, so the film makes no claim about what lifts anyone's regret. Its statement that remorse arises only in the two hate-rooted minds and only sometimes [C022-P:L149] is carried with C007. The line in L143 that brooding can make a weak wrong strong enough to lead to a lower destination is doctrinal teaching about results and is kept out of the voice under the kamma-as-fate floor.

C007 is where the sources place remorse, and that placement is the film's second argument. Pradeepika says envy, stinginess and remorse arise only in these two minds [C007-P:L51], both of which are always accompanied by painful feeling [C007-P:L25–L28]; aversion meets a disliked object and wants to be rid of it [C007-P:L32–L34]. Margaya names fear, dislike and discontent under the same word [C007-M:L3], and among the occasions for these minds lists sorrow over great wrongs done by one's own hand [C007-M:L19]. That is why beat 5 can say that regret of this kind is, in these texts, aversion turned on the past rather than conscience. The same Margaya line also classes grief at a parent's or child's death as hate-rooted; the digest's does_not_transfer forbids implying mourners are hateful, and this story contains a father's death, so only the clause about one's own wrong is used and no death is framed as a loss. The other does_not_transfer lines hold: no 'righteous anger' [C007-M:L11] and no 'anger only hurts yourself' reading, since the chronicle's own charge is harm to others; the bodily effects at [C007-P:L47] and the death-time destination at [C007-P:L51] are traditional teaching and are never narrated. The group's spent C007 lines (the two minds sorted by prompting; fear as recoil from a strong object; 'asked and refused'; the attacking enemy) are deliberately not used, although the chronicle's scene of a request refused would invite the third.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That these texts draw a line most of us do not. Remembering a wrong is not the problem; going over it, scorched, is, and the texts say that belief in the scorching as a payment is mistaken: it makes the wrong heavier and uses up the strength that could do good now. That they file this kind of regret with aversion, a pushing-away of one's own past, and not with conscience. And that a story can be told with the handbook's own images and still not be evidence of anyone's mind: the chronicle that describes this king was written generations later, in the textbook's order, and its translator doubted the deed at its centre.
what_must_be_real: The platform, the terraces, the slab bridge, the carving and any unfinished pieces are filmed as they stand, in their actual condition; nothing is cleared, wetted, dressed, moved or lit for the camera, and no equipment rests on the fabric. The rain is real rain; nothing is sprayed. No reconstruction of the temple, the king, the monks, the chronicle scene or a death, in image or sound; no frame composed to stand for a killing. The alleged parricide is stated once, attributed to the chronicle that carries it, with the translator's doubt beside it, and never adjudicated. The king is never narrated or framed as remorseful, anxious, angry or afraid: the chronicle's words for his state (anxiety, fear, fury, the snake) are reported only as the chronicle's, and only the snake is spoken, as a textbook image. What the same chronicle says followed (the turn to the Śaiva faith, the killing of monks, the burning of books, the transfer of a mountain's revenues) and its verdicts on the king's fate stay in the historical thread and are not spoken, and no image alludes to them. The tradition that a punishment ended the building is not repeated. No living person is filmed; if anyone is found making an offering at the site, filming stops.
position_hint: late in the group, after the films about anger and fear: the one film where the hate-rooted state is turned on one's own past, and where the charge in the story is visibly a later writer's. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the film say, or let a viewer conclude, that remorse cleanses or that suffering over a wrong is a payment, the reading the source itself rejects [C022-P:L143].
The opposite drift: implying that nobody should feel anything about what they did, when the source separates recalling, which it leaves alone, from scorching.

Diagnosing a dead king. The chronicle attributes anxiety, fear and fury to him; a later text's attribution is not a mental state the film can report, and none of those words may be spoken as fact or framed on anything.

Kamma as fate. The chronicle says he barred his way to heaven and fell under Māra; the nearest chronicle has him say the power of his merits had declined; the tradition Bell recorded has fire fall from hell while the work progressed; Pradeepika L143 and C007-P:L51 speak of lower destinations. All stay out of the voice, and the stopped building must never read as a verdict.

Entering a live religious topic. The chronicle's account of what the king did to the Order, and Geiger's note that the monks may have joined a conspiracy and invented the charge, both touch a subject that is still argued. They are recorded as layers in the historical thread only, never narrated, never as grievance and never as vindication.

Adjudicating the parricide by counting sources. Only one later chronicle asserts it; the nearest chronicle is silent, which is not a denial; a Portuguese Jesuit's reported denial was not read at source. The film states the charge and the translator's doubt and stops.

Bereavement register. The story contains a father's death, and Margaya classes grief at a parent's death as hate-rooted [C007-M:L19]; the film uses only the clause about one's own wrong and never frames a death as a loss.
Beauty swallowing the argument: wet carving in rain is seductive, and the circling could become a craft film with a voice laid over it.
Over-reading the circling. The repeated passes echo going over a thing again; the voice must not claim the wet stone 'is' heavier regret. It is a way of looking, not a demonstration.
Repeating the group's spent devices: no closing line about not reading a mind, no still drone hover, no zoom-out, no single unbroken move, no held uncomfortable frame, no real-time drip macro.
drop_if: No unfinished or half-dressed stone survives visibly at the site after the 2003 conservation, so the payoff cut has nothing to cut to (the fallback is the break between original stone and the brick repairs, which is weaker and must then be said to be modern).
The carved fillet, the spout and the other named carving are too weathered or overgrown to read on camera.
The Department of Archaeology will not permit filming inside the enclosure, or a drone over the river bend.
The site proves to be in active devotional use, so that a film with no worship in it could only be made by asking people to stop.

connections.note: That film's historical thread records this same king placing a sacred mountain in the charge of Śaiva ascetics after 1581 and a later king restoring Buddhist custody. It is the same king and the same later court that wrote down this film's accusation. Neither film speaks the other's episode: that transfer stays out of this film's voice, and this film's parricide is not in that one's.

Proposed in the group's blind selection as the film of an inscribed royal slab whose own text urges a man's removal. There the king's words are cut in stone; here the king left nothing written, every word about him is a later writer's, and the stone carries no text. This film is cut in circling passes in rain, not read along a surface in low sun.

selection.reason: Remorse is the one factor of the fourteen that asks to be seen as a thing done about the past, and this is the place where the island's record puts the question in so many words: a chronicle's 'how can I undo it?' and 'it cannot be undone', a building glossed as a redemption-temple, and a surveyor's finding that the building was stopped mid-work. The handbook's own answer, that going over a wrong makes it heavier and that remembering is not the fault, can be put on this footage without any living person being asked to admit anything, and the chronicle's textbook simile lets the film show a mind being written onto a king instead of reading one.

review.note: Rewritten whole on 2026-09-26. The previous body was pending, not confirmed or rejected, so no verdict is lost, but under standing decision 9 a replaced body would in any case reset the review. The location was fixed before writing: the brief for this rewrite was to test the story at this site in depth without changing the place, and to refuse if it could not carry the primary concept. It can. C022 is primary and the film is about remorse as the handbook defines it: not remembering a wrong, but the scorching over it, which the source says makes a wrong heavier rather than thinner. C007 is supporting and supplies the placement of remorse among the hate-rooted minds. The district cost is stated in suggested_location.research_note because district names are place names. Research corrections, all written into the historical thread: (1) the atonement story's earliest reachable attestation is H. C. P. Bell's 1904 district report, read at source for this record, which says Brahmins induced the king to build it; the Aritta Kivendu and 'diverting the river' versions are later and the chronicle usually credited with them does not contain them; (2) the same Bell sentence ends with fire falling from hell on the king while the work progressed, so the tradition is a punishment story and the film may not use it as a whole or in part (failure mode 8); (3) 'unfinished' is nevertheless supported independently by Bell's physical observation of half-dressed slabs and balustrade pieces lying where the work stopped, and is disputed by Percival's and Forbes's descriptions and by a contemporary Sinhala poem's description of a shrine in use; (4) there are two English translations of the chronicle passage (1889 and 1930) that differ in wording and in the order of events, and neither is averaged; (5) the 'paved canal to the river' of the site literature appears in Bell as a wide ditch or moat spanned by five stone slabs, joined to the river; (6) a popular claim that an English visitor saw the temple ruins in 1819 is wrong: Bell shows that account describes the Dutch fort across the river; (7) a newspaper date of 1849 for Portuguese destruction is impossible; (8) the author of the chronicle chapter is attributed by its translator 'in all probability', not certainly. The treatment is new for the group: a ground-level circling film in rain, cut in repeated passes, with a payoff cut from finished to unfinished stone. Still unverified: the present state of the unfinished pieces, permissions, and current use.

suggested_location.name: Berendi Kovil (Barendi / Barandi Kovila), Sītāvaka: the shrine platform, its three terraces and the slab bridge over the old ditch, in the bend of the Sītāvaka Ganga

also_known_as.name: Berendi Kovil / Barandi Kovila / Berandi Kovila
also_known_as.meaning: spelling variants in the archaeological, gazette and travel literature
also_known_as.used_by: Department of Archaeology; Sinhala and English usage

also_known_as.name: Bérendu Kovil
also_known_as.meaning: glossed by Bell (1904) as 'the temple to get redemption', of which he took the current name to be a corruption

also_known_as.name: Bairaindé Kovilla / Bhairava kovil
also_known_as.meaning: a shrine of Bhairava; Forbes's 1827 spelling, and a rival derivation of the name from Bhairava
also_known_as.used_by: Forbes 1827 (quoted by Bell); Sinhala popular writing

suggested_location.region: Kegalle District, Sabaragamuwa Province: Pahala Thalduwa (GN Division No. 118), Dehiovita Divisional Secretariat, on the right bank of the Sītāvaka Ganga immediately east of Avissawella town, which is across the river in Colombo District
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place where the record itself stages C022's question. A chronicle has a king ask how a wrong can be undone and his monks answer that it cannot; a surveyor glossed the building's name as 'the temple to get redemption'; and the same surveyor found the building stopped in mid-work. The handbook's teaching on remorse, that going over a wrong makes it heavier and that recalling it is not the fault, lands on that record without being forced, and the chronicle's own simile for the king is the handbook's simile for hate, which lets the film show a later writer composing a mind out of the textbook. It also films: carved stone of rare quality in the wettest country on the island, a river in spate on two sides, and a contrast between finished and unfinished stone that the camera can see without narration.

historical_thread.story:
Sītāvaka was the capital of a lowland kingdom created when the Kotte kingdom was divided in 1521; Māyādunnē held it until his death in 1581, and his son Rājasiṃha I until 1592/3. The shrine known as Berendi Kovil stands on a tongue of high land in a sharp bend of the Sītāvaka Ganga, across the river from the site of the palace. H. C. P. Bell described it in the Report on the Kegalla District (Archaeological Survey of Ceylon, Sessional Paper XIX of 1892, printed 1904), pp. 63–65, with a plan, an elevation and drawings of the spout and a pillar. From the road one crosses a wide ditch spanned by five stone slabs 14 ft 4 in long and 1 ft 10 in thick; the ditch joins the river on the right and loses itself in low land on the left. Three earthwork terraces follow, skirted by the river on the right and rear: the lowest 280 by 60 ft, the second 180 by 45 ft, the third 4 ft 8 in high and revetted in six courses of smoothed stone with an undercut double-flexure coping. Steps rose in the centre of each bank, with monolithic doorframes at the top, of which one carved jamb still stood. The shrine rises from a paved basement; its dado and cornice carry water-leaves and small makara-toranas, and a fillet carved with a string of circular and star-shaped flowers runs round the wall. A spout finished as a lotus projects from the left side of the platform. The usable area inside the four walls was only 15 ft 6 in square. Two small slabs carved with a vase on a lotus stand lay to the left of the building. Bell judged the style Dravidian, with its ornament 'soft and chaste'.

Bell's most important observation for this film is archaeological, not traditional: 'That the work at Berendi Kóvil was suddenly stopped whilst in progress is attested by the pieces of massive volute balustrades (8 ft. 6 in. by 6 ft. 9 in. when united), a huge oval "moonstone," and many half-dressed slabs, which lie about. What the ultimate intention of the architect was, may never be known.' In the same paragraph he writes that the Portuguese swept away walls and columns 'if the temple ever rose above its platform', and that the 'pillars' and 'inscriptions' reported by earlier visitors were not there. He also records a stone altar, moulded in seven courses and called hat-māl-gala, carried from the site on a bamboo raft and lying all but buried in the mud at the ferry.

The earlier notices Bell quotes do not agree with each other or with him. Robert Percival, 20 March 1800: the ruins of a temple, 'the first built of stone which I had seen on the Island', walls four or five feet high with a flight of steps all round, and 'several inscriptions' visible on the flags and pillars. Forbes, 1827: the remains of the 'Bairaindé Kovilla, erected for demon worship by Rája Sinha about the middle of the sixteenth century', within several quadrilateral enclosures, about thirty feet long, of handsome carved pillars supporting a cornice. H. White (Orientalist IV, p. 35): a number of the stones had been carried away for building. C. J. R. Le Mesurier, 7 October 1885: 'the remains of an ancient unfinished temple (so it was said, but I was unable to find any one who could give me an intelligent account of it)', on registered temple land, part of whose stone a lessee had used to build 'a nice little house'. F. H. Price, 17 May 1887, called it 'built about the middle of the sixteenth century by Rája Sinha, the apostate'.

The accusation belongs to the Cūḷavaṃsa, chapter 93, verses 4–14. Wilhelm Geiger's translation (English by C. Mabel Rickmers, 1930, Part II pp. 224–226) reads that Rājasiha, 'the great fool, even slew his own father'; that one day, after almsgiving, he 'asked the Grand theras full of anxiety: "How can I undo the crime of my father's murder?"'; that the theras expounded the doctrine but 'could not win over the wicked mind of this fool' and said 'To undo the committed crime is impossible'; that 'full of fury like some terrible poisonous snake which has been struck by a stick' he asked the adherents of Śiva, received their answer that it was possible 'like ambrosia', smeared his body with ashes and adopted their religion; and that he then 'annihilated the Order', slew monks, burned books, destroyed monasteries, placed Śaiva ascetics on the sacred mountain to take its revenues, and that bhikkhus left the Order 'through fear of the King'. The chapter closes with verdicts on his fate. The 1889 English translation, as Bell quotes it (XCIII 2–11), has him slay his father 'with his own hand', be 'seized with fear', ask 'How can I absolve myself from the sin of killing a father?', hear that 'The consequence of a sin that hath been committed cannot be destroyed', and put the priests to death before, not after, turning to the followers of Śiva. Geiger attributes chapters 90.104 to 100 'in all probability' to Tibbotuvāve, Mahānāyaka of the Malvatu vihāra, entrusted by Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha with completing the chronicle, and says his contribution was composed in that king's praise and during his lifetime. The same simile, the smitten snake, is the commentarial definition of hate (dosa) in the Abhidhamma tradition, and Pradeepika uses it.

Geiger's own notes dissent. On v. 4: 'Whether Rájasíha ... was really his father's murderer, may be doubted.' On v. 9: the motives given for the conversion 'scarcely accord with the facts'; he states that the Buddhist clergy had joined a conspiracy against the king and that 'these clerics may also have invented the murder', citing P. E. Pieris and W. F. Gunawardhana's 'Raja Sinha I, Parricide and Centenarian' (JRAS CB XVIII, 1905). On 94.5, where the next king's accession follows the death of 'the slayer of his father', Geiger notes that the epithet there refers not to Māyādunnē but to Vīrasundara, the new king's own father, whom Rājasiṃha had had killed. The Rājāvaliya (B. Gunasekara's translation, 1900), a Sinhala prose chronicle, says only 'King Mayadunne died after he had reigned 70 years'; it records no parricide, no conversion, no persecution and no kovil. It names Aritta Kivendu Perumāl once, as one of some fakirs from the Soli country, made Mannamperuma Mohotti and given 'the daughter of the Rajahetti, who had been the king's concubine'.

The atonement tradition's earliest reachable attestation is Bell, p. 63: 'Local tradition adds that the Brahmins induced Rája Sinha (I., 1581–92 A.D.) to build the Hindú Kóvil, since known as Berendi (a corruption of Bérendu, "the temple to get redemption"), and that as the work was progressing fire fell from hell and took the apostate monarch to his own place.' Later retellings add a named adviser, a diverted river (a Daily Mirror feature reproduced by amazinglanka, which credits the Rājāvaliya), or, in a 2018 Sinhala newspaper feature, a start date of 1582, a plan of seven storeys, 20,000 men working for twenty years, and an adviser who arranged that it could never be finished.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C022's question is what a person is doing when they go back over a wrong, and this site's record asks it in words. The chronicle's king asks how the deed can be undone; the monks say it cannot; the building is glossed as a temple 'to get redemption'. The handbook's answer is a third position neither side of that exchange holds: recalling the wrong is not the fault, and the scorching over it, which many people take for a good quality that thins the wrong, fouls the mind again and again and makes a small wrong heavy, while grieving over good not done produces no good [C022-P:L143]. The film can therefore say something about payment without saying anything about the king.

The chronicle then hands the film its safeguard. Having staged the question, it describes the questioner as a poisonous snake struck by a stick, which is Pradeepika's simile for hate [C022-P:L119] and the standard commentarial one. The page is not a report; it is a learned monk, writing generations later under another dynasty, assembling a king's mind out of the textbook: a question about undoing, a refusal, then the image for hate. That lets the group's charge land on the looking, on the literature that has gone over this story for four centuries, and never on anyone in frame.

C007 fixes where the state lives. The sources place remorse only in the two hate-rooted minds [C007-P:L51; C022-P:L149], always with painful feeling [C007-P:L25–L28], and Margaya lists sorrow over great wrongs done by one's own hand among the occasions of that mind [C007-M:L19]. On these texts' own terms, then, regret of this kind is aversion turned on one's own past, not conscience, which is why it cannot be a payment.

The building supplies what no analogy could: finished carving beside half-dressed slabs, a payment begun in stone and stopped, for a debt that is not established. Bell's reading of the stone (work suddenly stopped; intention unknown) is evidence the camera can see; the tradition's reading (a punishment from hell) is exactly the kamma-as-fate reading the floor forbids, and the film shows the stone and declines the tradition. Remembering the story, and not knowing whether it happened, is the exempt case: ordinary uncertainty about what one cannot settle is not the unwholesome doubt [C022-P:L179; C022-M:L57].
what_is_certain: The site is in Kegalle District: OSM places the archaeological-site node (6.95515, 80.22411) in Talduwa, Kegalle District; the gazette protecting the approach bridge names GN Division No. 118 Pahala Thalduwa, Dehiovita DS; Bell described it in his Kegalla District report. Avissawella town, across the river, is in Colombo District.

Bell (1904, pp. 63–65, read at source) describes: a ditch spanned by five slabs 14 ft 4 in long; three terraces (280 × 60 ft, 180 × 45 ft, and a third 4 ft 8 in high revetted in six courses); steps and monolithic doorframes, one carved jamb upright; a paved basement and platform with water-leaf mouldings, makara-toranas and a fillet of circular and star-shaped flowers; a lotus-finished spout on the left side; an interior of 15 ft 6 in square; two small slabs carved with a vase; Dravidian style.

Bell writes that the work 'was suddenly stopped whilst in progress', citing pieces of massive volute balustrades, a huge oval moonstone and many half-dressed slabs lying about, and that 'what the ultimate intention of the architect was, may never be known'.
Bell found no pillars and no inscriptions at the site, and records a seven-course stone altar (hat-māl-gala) taken from it by bamboo raft and lying in the mud at the ferry.
Le Mesurier (1885) was told it was 'an ancient unfinished temple' but found nobody who could explain it; stone from it had been used to build a house (Bell's plan marks a house within the enclosure).

Cūḷavaṃsa 93.4–14 (Geiger/Rickmers 1930, Part II pp. 224–226, read at source) contains the parricide charge, the question 'How can I undo the crime of my father's murder?', the theras' answer 'To undo the committed crime is impossible', the snake-struck-by-a-stick simile, the conversion, and the persecution.

Geiger's notes to the same passage say the parricide 'may be doubted', that the stated motives for the conversion 'scarcely accord with the facts', and that the charge may have been invented; his note to 94.5 says the epithet 'slayer of his father' there refers to Vīrasundara.

Geiger attributes chapters 90.104–100 'in all probability' to Tibbotuvāve, entrusted by Kīrti Śrī Rājasiṃha with completing the chronicle, and says that contribution was written in that king's praise.

The Rājāvaliya (Gunasekara 1900, read at source) says only that Māyādunnē 'died after he had reigned 70 years', and records no parricide, conversion, persecution or kovil; it names Aritta Kivendu Perumāl once, as a fakir from the Soli country made Mannamperuma Mohotti.

The earliest attestation reached for the atonement tradition is Bell 1904, p. 63, as local tradition: Brahmins induced the king to build it; the name is glossed 'the temple to get redemption'; and fire from hell took the king while the work progressed.
Pradeepika's simile for hate is a snake struck with a stick [C022-P:L119]; the Abhidhamma commentarial definition of dosa uses the same smitten-snake image.
The stone bridge on the way to the kovil is a protected monument, Gazette No. 1486 of 23 February 2007.
what_is_disputed: Whether Rājasiṃha I killed his father. Asserted by Cūḷavaṃsa 93, written about 170 years later, and reportedly by the Minor Rājāvaliya; doubted by the chronicle's translator; the Rājāvaliya is silent, which is not a denial; Fernão de Queyroz is reported (Wikipedia, not read at source) to say Māyādunnē died naturally; the Dutch envoy Spilbergen is reported to have found the rumour circulating only in the Kandyan kingdom in 1602 (secondary, not read). Unresolved.

The wording of the chronicle scene. The 1889 translation has 'with his own hand', 'seized with fear', 'absolve myself from the sin', 'The consequence of a sin ... cannot be destroyed', and the priests killed before the turn to Śiva; Geiger's 1930 translation has 'full of anxiety', 'undo the crime', 'To undo the committed crime is impossible', and the persecution after the conversion. Both are recorded; neither is averaged. The film quotes only the question and the answer, in Geiger's wording.

Whether the building was ever finished. For 'stopped in progress': Bell's half-dressed slabs and balustrade pieces; Le Mesurier's informants; the Bell tradition and a 2018 newspaper feature. Against, or complicating: Percival (1800) saw walls four or five feet high with steps all round and inscriptions; Forbes (1827) saw carved pillars supporting a cornice; Bell himself allows that the Portuguese swept walls and columns away 'if the temple ever rose above its platform'; and a Sinhala blog identifies it with the 'Bhairava kovil' across the river from the palace, with dance offerings and wall paintings, described in the Sävul Sandesaya of the Sītāvaka period, an identification not checked against the poem. The film says only what Bell saw lying there.

Who built it and when. Popular accounts: Rājasiṃha I (1581–1593), or his father Māyādunnē, or earlier; a 2018 newspaper gives 1582 as the start; an unattributed claim assigns the carving style to the Polonnaruwa period while the same literature calls it Vijayanagara or Dravidian. Bell and Forbes say the middle of the sixteenth century.

To whom it was dedicated: Śiva (provincial tourism site; a Sinhala newspaper), Kālī (Lankapradeepa, following site literature), Bhairava ('demon worship', Forbes 1827; the blog's reading of the Sandesaya). Not settled.

How it came down: swept away by the Portuguese (Forbes; Bell, conditionally); dismantled for building stone (White; Le Mesurier; Lankapradeepa); a 2018 newspaper's date of '1849' for Portuguese destruction is impossible on its own terms, since the Portuguese had left two centuries earlier.

The meaning of the name: Bérendu, 'the temple to get redemption' (Bell, from tradition), or a corruption of Bhairava / Bairaindé (Forbes's spelling; Sinhala popular writing). Both are after-the-fact etymologies.

The atonement story's details. Bell's tradition names Brahmins; later versions name Aritta Kivendu Perumāl, add a diverted river (credited wrongly to the Rājāvaliya), or add the drowning of 120 monks and a building designed never to be finished (2018 newspaper). The Rājāvaliya contains none of it.

The water feature. Site literature (Abeyawardana 2002 via Lankapradeepa) describes a stone-paved canal linking the kovil to the river; Bell describes a wide ditch spanned by slabs, joined to the river, and the provincial tourism site speaks of a moat on the west. Probably one feature; not checked on the ground.
A 2018 newspaper says an English visitor saw scattered ruins of the kovil in 1819. Bell shows that the 1819 account describes the Dutch fort on the other bank. Not used.

The chronicle's own verdicts on the king (barring his way to heaven, falling under Māra), the Rājāvaliya's line in his mouth that 'the power of my merits has declined', and Bell's tradition of fire from hell are recorded here as documents. All are kamma-as-fate material and are excluded from the film.
The authorship of the chapter is Geiger's 'in all probability' attribution to Tibbotuvāve, not a certainty.

what_to_film: The river bend from a low drone moving with the current, rain approaching and again after it: the tongue of land, the water on two sides, the platform only glimpsed in the trees. No hover, no climb.

The platform's carved basement in repeated low passes on a 35–50 mm lens, each starting at the lotus-tipped spout: water-leaf mouldings, the fillet of circular and star-shaped flowers, the upright carved jamb, the two vase slabs, going darker with each pass as the squall comes in.
The half-dressed slabs, balustrade fragments and oval threshold stone Bell recorded, if they are still there, framed where they lie, wet.
The finished flower fillet in close frame, for the payoff cut to an uncarved slab.
The terraces, one static frame each, and the old ditch on its bridge of five long slabs, full after rain.
The 2003 brick repairs beside the original stone, shown honestly as the site's condition.
The river leaving the bend, from the low drone, downstream, as the ending.
suggested_location.access: A short signposted lane off the Avissawella–Hatton (A7) road just east of the bridge over the Sītāvaka Ganga, about 50 km from Colombo; Bell put the ruin within 200 yards of the bridge. It is a fenced archaeological site with a Department of Archaeology signboard. Filming inside a declared archaeological area needs Department of Archaeology permission, and the drone needs both that and civil aviation clearance; the palace site across the river is separately gazetted. The terraces are steep earth banks, slippery in rain, and the river is dangerous in spate: no crew member goes to the water's edge. No permission, contact or access arrangement has been sought.
suggested_location.best_time: An inter-monsoon afternoon in April–May or October–November: squalls in the early afternoon, the river high by late afternoon. The platform passes are shot as the rain arrives and at its height; the payoff cut and the final drone as it clears. Avoid direct sun. January is the driest fallback, with a lower river and pale stone throughout, which weakens the passes.

suggested_location.research_note:
District, in plain words: this film puts Kegalle District at seven films, which the slate's own rule treats as closed. Chathura explicitly allowed Kegalle to go to seven for this one story, because it is the only place found where the record itself asks C022's question (a chronicle's 'how can this be undone?' and 'it cannot', a building glossed as a redemption-temple and found stopped mid-work), and the story exists nowhere else; the site cannot be moved, and filming it 'from the Colombo bank' would be a cheat, since the ruin is on the Kegalle side. Live count before this film: 6 (IDEA-0080, 0102, 0121, 0133, 0146, 0179); after: 7. The superseded body of IDEA-0221 also names this site and must be refilled elsewhere, or Kegalle would read 8 and the site would be used twice. The district was checked, not assumed: OSM reverse geocoding of the archaeological-site node gives Talduwa, Kegalle District; the gazette entry for the approach bridge gives Pahala Thalduwa, Dehiovita DS; Bell filed it in his Kegalla report. Travel sites that file it under Avissawella, Colombo District or the Western Province are misled by the town across the river.

What was read at source for this record: Bell's Report on the Kegalla District pp. 62–65 and plates (archive.org scan, no text layer, read page by page as images); Cūḷavaṃsa 93–94 with Geiger's notes, and his notes on authorship at 90.102 and 100 (Geiger/Rickmers 1930, archive.org OCR); the Rājāvaliya in Gunasekara's 1900 translation (searched in full for the reign, the parricide, the conversion, monks and a kovil); the Pradeepika and Margaya source lines cited. Corrections to the briefing material: (1) the atonement story is not in the Rājāvaliya; its earliest reachable attestation is Bell 1904, where it is local tradition naming Brahmins, not Aritta Kivendu, and has no diverted river; (2) Bell's tradition ends with fire from hell taking the king while the work progressed, so 'unfinished' in the tradition is part of a punishment story and cannot be used alone (failure mode 8); the film uses only Bell's separate physical observation of half-dressed slabs; (3) the briefing's 'unfinished' was not in Bell's hands a certainty: Percival and Forbes describe walls, steps and pillars, and Bell allows the temple may or may not have risen above its platform; (4) two English translations of the chronicle passage differ in wording and in the order of conversion and killing, and the selection note's quotation follows Geiger only; (5) the 'stone-paved canal to the river' corresponds in Bell to a moat or ditch spanned by five slabs; the earlier draft's idea of a descent along a paved channel from the terraces to the river is not supported by Bell and is dropped; (6) the claim that an English visitor saw the kovil ruins in 1819 misreads an account of the Dutch fort; (7) a newspaper's '1849' Portuguese destruction is impossible; (8) the chapter's author is Geiger's probable attribution, not a certainty; (9) Bell reports no inscriptions and no pillars, against Percival's inscriptions. The carvings of an elephant and a parrot reported in travel writing are not in Bell and are not used.

Current religious use: nothing found indicates worship at the ruin; every source describes a ruin or archaeological site, and no source mentions offerings, a priest or festivals. Geiger's 1930 note that the king was then receiving divine honours locally under another name is a separate matter, unverified today, and kept out of the film. The 1885 lease of the land under a Kandyan temple is recorded history and is not entered in the film.

Not verified: Queyroz, Spilbergen, the Minor Rājāvaliya and the Sävul Sandesaya were not read; Gunawardhana 1905 was not obtained; the commentarial smitten-snake definition of dosa was reached through a secondary encyclopedia quotation, not the Visuddhimagga or Atthasālinī text. Whether the half-dressed slabs, balustrade pieces and oval stone Bell saw survive after the 2003 conservation is unknown, and the payoff depends on it. Current access, signage, permissions and the state of the carving are unchecked.

Images: the Commons search API was queried with a descriptive user agent for Berendi Kovil, Barandi Kovil, Berandi, Barandi Kovila, Sitawaka/Seethawaka kovil, Avissawella temple ruins, Sitawaka, Seethawaka, Avissawella, the river under three spellings and Rajasinha. Commons holds no photograph of the monument or of the river bend. The one image carried is confirmed by action=query&titles=File:Seethawaka_Wet_Zone.jpg&prop=imageinfo, is categorised under Seethawaka Botanical Garden, and is captioned in capitals as not the site. Bell's plan, elevation and spout drawing are in the archive.org scan and are the best available record of what the film would see.

unknowns: Whether the half-dressed slabs, the volute balustrade pieces and the oval threshold stone Bell recorded still lie at the site after the 2003 conservation; the payoff cut depends on them.
Whether the flower fillet, the spout and the vase slabs are legible after conservation and a century of wet-zone weathering.
Department of Archaeology permission for filming in the enclosure, and drone clearance over the river bend; none sought.
Whether anyone makes offerings at the ruin today. Nothing found suggests it, but it has not been checked on the ground.
Queyroz, Spilbergen, the Minor Rājāvaliya, the Sävul Sandesaya and Gunawardhana 1905 were not read; everything attributed to them is second-hand and none of it is used in the voice.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. Under standing decision 2 the location is recorded as proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review verdict. The historical thread is desk research: Bell 1904, the Cūḷavaṃsa in Geiger's translation and the Rājāvaliya in Gunasekara's were read at source; everything else is marked as secondary or unread. No scene or shot is decided here.
